title: Hiragana
subtitle: The 46 basic characters of the Japanese syllabary

cards.note: Picture an apple with a cross stuck through it, and someone saying "ah!". Don't confuse it with お (o), which has a small extra stroke at the top right.
Two strokes side by side, like two eels swimming: i sounds like the "ee" in "eel". In り (ri) the right stroke is much longer.
Someone bent over, holding their stomach and groaning "ooh", with a small tuft of hair on top. Compare ら (ra), whose main stroke starts with a short vertical line.
An energetic dancer with a feather on her head, kicking out a leg: e as in "energetic". The bottom of the stroke ends in a zigzag.
Like あ, but with a small extra stroke at the top right, as if someone were shouting "Oh!".
A karate fighter with a staff shouting "Ka!"; the small stroke on the right is the shout. With two dots (が) it becomes ga.
Looks like an old key with its bit at the bottom: ki sounds like "key". Two crossbars make ki, only one makes さ (sa).
The open beak of a cuckoo calling "coo coo". If the angle lies flat like a roof, it is へ (he).
A post on the left and a keg hanging from a pole on the right: ke as in "keg". If the right stroke ends in a loop, it is は (ha).
Two strokes stacked like two koi carp in a pond. Add a vertical stroke on the left and it becomes に (ni).
Like き, but with only one crossbar: a samurai sword slicing across. The bottom curve bulges to the left, like a c.
A fishhook, and she (shi) is fishing with it. Hepburn romanization writes shi because it sounds like "she", not "see".
A swing with a loop in its rope: you swoop through the air on it. The final u is often barely audible, so desu sounds like "dess".
A sail on a mast with a long boom across it: se as in "sail".
A zigzag like a stitched seam: sew (so) it up. Some people write the top part as a separate stroke; both are correct.
A lowercase t on the left and a lopsided a on the right: together, ta. Compare な (na), which has a loop at the bottom right.
Like さ, but the curve bulges to the right, like a round belly full of chips. Pronounced like the "chee" in "cheese".
One big wave, like a tsunami. Written small (っ), it doubles the following consonant, as in きって (kitte, postage stamp).
A T with a curved stem, like an outstretched hand (te also means hand, 手).
A toe with a splinter stuck in it. As a particle, と links nouns like "and": 犬と猫, dog and cat.
A nun (na) kneeling next to a cross, her robe forming the loop at the bottom. Think of た with a loop.
A vertical stroke next to こ, like a knee (ni) next to two bones. As a particle, に marks a destination or a point in time.
A bowl of noodles with a fork, the noodle curling into a loop at the bottom. Without the loop it is め (me).
A cat (neko) with a curled-up tail. ね, れ and わ begin the same way; only the ending tells them apart: loop, kick, curve.
Looks like a no-entry sign: No! As a particle, の shows possession: 私の本 means "my book".
Like け, but with a loop at the bottom right, as if someone were laughing "ha ha". As the topic particle, は is pronounced "wa".
A wide, grinning mouth giggling "hee hee".
Mount Fuji with small clouds on the left and right. The sound lies between f and h: you blow air through your lips, and your teeth do not touch your lip as in an English f.
A flat mountain: "Hey, let's climb that!" へ looks almost the same in hiragana and katakana. As the direction particle, it is pronounced "e".
Like は, but with an extra crossbar on top, like a house with a roof: ho as in "home".
A mast with two crossbars and a loop at the bottom. Ma is also the word 間, the deliberate pause this app is named after.
A loop with a long tail, like a musical note: do, re, mi.
A cow with a loop for a belly and a dot for an ear, going "moo". Don't confuse it with す (su), which has no dot.
An eye with lashes, and me (目) really does mean eye. With a loop at the end it becomes ぬ (nu).
A fishhook with two crossbars: more (mo) bait. As a particle, も means "also".
A yak with curved horns. Written small (ゃ), it combines with the syllable before it, as in きゃ (kya).
Looks like a fish swimming in hot water. Yu (湯) means hot water, and the curtain at a hot spring bath often bears this character.
A yo-yo hanging from its string. At the end of a sentence, よ emphasizes new information: そうですよ, "that's right, trust me".
A crouching rabbit (ra) with one ear sticking up on top. The Japanese r lies somewhere between r, l and d.
Like い, but the right stroke is long, like a river (ri) flowing downward.
Ends in a loop at the bottom, like the curled tail of a kangaroo (roo). Without the loop it becomes ろ (ro).
Like ね, but the stroke ends in a kick to the right instead of a loop, like a leg stretched out to rest (re).
Like る, but without the loop at the end: a road (ro) with no roundabout.
Like ね and れ, but ending on the right in an open, soft curve like a wave (wa). 和 (wa), by the way, means harmony.
Appears almost only as the object particle and is then pronounced "o": 水を飲む, to drink water.
Looks like a lowercase n in cursive. It is the only character made of a consonant alone, and no standard word begins with it.
